title: Replicants examine what deployment readiness requires — November 10, 2026: Business
lead: Demonstration collection, changed conditions and site requirements shape the path from project to service.

news.title: RobotBank starts its own quadruped programme with site conditions still to validate
news.summary: Tokyo-based RobotBank announced an industrial quadruped for inspection applications. Sales timing and specifications remain undefined, while the company listed the criteria it intends to assess during future operation.
news.details: Tokyo-based RobotBank announced development of its own industrial quadruped on November 9. Intended uses include inspection rounds around production equipment, observation in logistics and large facilities, and infrastructure inspection support. The company plans to validate site-specific conditions before fixing product specifications. Mechanical design, locomotion control, sensors, teleoperation and maintenance will be considered together. Environmental recognition and autonomous task execution are planned as staged additions following technical validation, rather than established capabilities of an available machine.

news.limitations: Development start and validation plan; specifications, measured results, price and release timing are not announced.
news.evidence_status: Official developer or vendor announcement; figures and plans are not independent evaluation.
news.body:
An inspection customer needs more than the ability to cross uneven ground. Sensor choice, operator assistance and servicing costs at a particular site also matter. RobotBank places those issues alongside mechanical development. The announcement reveals intended product criteria, although it does not yet allow selection of a finished configuration or calculation of a purchase budget.

Tokyo-based RobotBank announced development of its own industrial quadruped on November 9. Intended uses include inspection rounds around production equipment, observation in logistics and large facilities, and infrastructure inspection support. The company plans to validate site-specific conditions before fixing product specifications. Mechanical design, locomotion control, sensors, teleoperation and maintenance will be considered together. Environmental recognition and autonomous task execution are planned as staged additions following technical validation, rather than established capabilities of an available machine.

RobotBank stresses that this is not its first development effort: the project builds on previous robot products, software platforms and system integration. Through RobotBank Lab, it plans to analyse customer needs, produce prototypes and conduct trials. Proposed assessment criteria include task success, operating time, frequency of human intervention, safety and maintenance expense. No measured results for those criteria, final specifications, sales date or mass-production schedule are supplied. Mobile manipulators and other possible follow-on products are identified as areas for consideration, not a guaranteed product roadmap. The release describes the start of a development programme, not a completed deployment.

Specifications and timing are explicitly left open, and subsequent robot types are candidates rather than commitments to bring each one to market.

news.title: HumansX offers a demonstration-collection setup, beyond individual robot hands
news.summary: Tokyo's HumansX proposed a dual-arm installation with operator gloves for recording demonstrations. Complete-system pricing and delivery depend on configuration; the next hand batch is expected from February 2027.
news.details: Tokyo-based HumansX proposed a dual-arm data-collection system on November 9, combining Wuji Hand 2 robotic hands with Wuji Glove operator gloves. Operator movements can be recorded as demonstrations for later robot learning. Each hand has 20 actively controlled degrees of freedom, meaning separate movement directions, with four per finger. Vendor specifications give a mass of about 800 grams and fingertip peak force of at least 12 newtons. Peak force is not a continuous-load rating or the mass of an object that can safely be held.

news.engineering_impact: Hand delivery and complete-system delivery require separate agreement. A vendor's fully reserved allocation supplies neither customer count nor revenue or the number of installations working today. The claim of lower cost also comes without a comparative budget. Commercial assessment therefore depends on the chosen configuration, support and on-site work included in the offer.
news.limitations: Vendor specifications; no independent lifetime test, fixed public complete-system price or autonomous-learning outcome from collected demonstrations.
news.evidence_status: Official developer or vendor announcement; figures and plans are not independent evaluation.
news.body:
An applied project can stall before model training while a customer connects hands, gloves and movement recording. HumansX addresses that stage. The contract can therefore extend beyond buying a hand: readiness to collect useful demonstrations after setup needs to be defined, rather than assumed from the inventory of purchased components.

Vendor specifications give a mass of about 800 grams and fingertip peak force of at least 12 newtons. Peak force is not a continuous-load rating or the mass of an object that can safely be held.

The assembled configuration uses Marvin Pro arms. The supplier offers setup, on-site installation and Japanese-language support. The first hand allocation is fully reserved; the next batch is scheduled to ship from February 2027. Its own website opened second-batch reservations on November 6: the November 9 release adds the dual-arm system offering, rather than establishing immediate off-the-shelf availability. Price and delivery for a complete installation depend on configuration and require an enquiry. The announcement supplies neither an independent hand-lifetime test nor evidence that collected demonstrations have already enabled autonomous completion of a customer's task.

news.title: DexBench tests whether a robot skill survives changed working conditions
news.summary: RLWRLD introduced 15 DexBench tasks for simulated evaluation of robotic hands in Seoul. The suite tests unfamiliar objects and conditions, while correspondence with physical operation remains to be validated.
news.details: RLWRLD introduced DexBench at NVIDIA AI Day Seoul at the COEX convention centre on November 9. It is a suite of repeatable tests for dexterous manipulation, meaning precise robotic hand work with objects. This first major release from an initiative started with NVIDIA in June contains 15 tasks across retail, logistics, assembly and hotel food-and-beverage operations. Examples include retrieving products from shelves, unloading roll cages, inserting connectors, fastening screws, stacking plates and pouring liquids. Virtual objects and equipment are modelled using specifications of real products.

news.body:
Deployment depends on the gap between an attractive demonstration and retained performance after products or workstations change. DexBench addresses that gap through shared tests. A customer can use this approach to frame supplier questions, but a test launch does not supply a universal threshold for accepting a machine into industrial operation.

RLWRLD introduced DexBench at NVIDIA AI Day Seoul at the COEX convention centre on November 9. It is a suite of repeatable tests for dexterous manipulation, meaning precise robotic hand work with objects. This first major release from an initiative started with NVIDIA in June contains 15 tasks across retail, logistics, assembly and hotel food-and-beverage operations. Examples include retrieving products from shelves, unloading roll cages, inserting connectors, fastening screws, stacking plates and pouring liquids. Virtual objects and equipment are modelled using specifications of real products.

Evaluation goes beyond whether a task worked once. Conditions change along three dimensions: objects, physical properties and spatial arrangements. That probes transfer to situations not encountered during training. The foundation is Isaac Lab-Arena, software for evaluating robot-control policies at scale, together with Newton's physical-interaction simulation. RLWRLD plans to release code, environments, data, baseline models and a leaderboard. Comparing simulated performance with physical robots is identified as further work. Launching a test suite therefore does not establish the operational reliability of any particular robot at an actual industrial site.

A contract should preserve a simulation score's identity and conditions. Changes in products, friction or position may alter data and configuration requirements. While comparison with physical robots remains a future stage, virtual evaluation can compare development choices. It cannot substitute for acceptance at a particular line with its own failures and operating expenses.

news.title: NVIDIA's new training tools still leave customer acceptance to measure
news.summary: NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL for robot learning. It reports success changing with demonstration count and a separate training-throughput gain, rather than a completed deployment cost model.
news.details: At the November 9 Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, a trained robot-control program using a representation of the physical world, alongside new simulation tools. According to the company, the model completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations. That counts tasks achieved, not successful attempts. With one demonstration per task, average success was 71%; with five it reached 95%. Training used diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of open human video recorded from the wearer's viewpoint.
news.technical_novelty: At the November 9 Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, a trained robot-control program using a representation of the physical world, alongside new simulation tools. According to the company, the model completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations. That counts tasks achieved, not successful attempts. With one demonstration per task, average success was 71%; with five it reached 95%. Training used diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of open human video recorded from the wearer's viewpoint.
news.engineering_impact: Without task-specific demonstrations does not mean training without data: large robot and human datasets already underpin the model. Computing-time savings also refer to a particular simulation configuration. The percentages and throughput multiplier alone do not yield the combined cost of demonstrations, integration and acceptance trials at a specific workstation.
news.limitations: Developer-reported results on selected tasks and configurations; no independent reproduction or customer-workstation throughput calculation.
news.evidence_status: Official developer or vendor announcement; figures and plans are not independent evaluation.
news.body:
If one example and five examples produce different outcomes, preparing data remains part of deployment cost. NVIDIA's figures are particularly useful when read beside their conditions. The tools may change an experimental plan, but a customer still needs to establish how many demonstrations its operation requires and which failure rate it can tolerate.

At the November 9 Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, NVIDIA introduced GR00T 2, a trained robot-control program using a representation of the physical world, alongside new simulation tools. According to the company, the model completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations. That counts tasks achieved, not successful attempts. With one demonstration per task, average success was 71%; with five it reached 95%. Training used diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of open human video recorded from the wearer's viewpoint.

The same programme introduced Isaac Lab 3.0, software for training robots. Researchers can choose between PhysX and Newton physics solvers; Newton can model deformable objects such as cloth and cables. In a particular vision-based dexterous-manipulation training benchmark, the Newton configuration provided up to 2.5 times the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 with PhysX. This compares two training configurations, not physical robot speed. The developer reports all these figures. The announcement does not establish the same performance on arbitrary hardware or provide independent reproduction of the results.

Without task-specific demonstrations does not mean training without data: large robot and human datasets already underpin the model. Computing-time savings also refer to a particular simulation configuration. The percentages and throughput multiplier alone do not yield the combined cost of demonstrations, integration and acceptance trials at a specific workstation.

news.title: Physical cart pushing is demonstrated, while warehouse economics remain unmeasured
news.summary: Huazhong University researchers transferred ForPC from simulation to a Unitree G1. The machine pushed a cart carrying up to 30 kilograms, but a flat-floor trial does not establish warehouse throughput.
news.details: ZhenYu Zou and colleagues at Huazhong University of Science and Technology proposed ForPC, whole-body control for humanoid cart pushing. First the robot learns balance under hand loads and different upper-body poses. A supplementary controller then adjusts the arms, waist and legs using estimates of robot–cart interaction inferred from the robot's own signals rather than external force sensors. Both arms should contribute to propulsion instead of wasting effort by opposing each other on the same handle. The method treats walking and sustained hand contact as a coupled problem.
news.technical_novelty: ZhenYu Zou and colleagues at Huazhong University of Science and Technology proposed ForPC, whole-body control for humanoid cart pushing. First the robot learns balance under hand loads and different upper-body poses. A supplementary controller then adjusts the arms, waist and legs using estimates of robot–cart interaction inferred from the robot's own signals rather than external force sensors. Both arms should contribute to propulsion instead of wasting effort by opposing each other on the same handle. The method treats walking and sustained hand contact as a coupled problem.
news.engineering_impact: Thirty kilograms describes cargo on wheels, not a mass lifted by the hands. That distinction changes mechanical requirements and comparisons with other transport options. Floor and route properties, loading arrangements and human assistance still need evaluation. The source supplies no cost per trip, shift-level statistics or customer-site fleet-availability assessment.
news.limitations: Author-run flat indoor-floor tests using a visual cart-heading marker. Lifetime, cost per trip and slope operation were not measured.
news.evidence_status: Research preprint and author-run experiments; independent reproduction has not been confirmed.
news.organization: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
news.body:
Using an ordinary wheeled cart is attractive where existing material flow already accommodates it. The robot must handle more than its own body, however: cargo changes hand reactions and balance. ForPC studies that interaction. It provides a physical demonstration to discuss when choosing a pilot, without a published profitability calculation for a transport service.

ZhenYu Zou and colleagues at Huazhong University of Science and Technology proposed ForPC, whole-body control for humanoid cart pushing. First the robot learns balance under hand loads and different upper-body poses. A supplementary controller then adjusts the arms, waist and legs using estimates of robot–cart interaction inferred from the robot's own signals rather than external force sensors. Both arms should contribute to propulsion instead of wasting effort by opposing each other on the same handle. The method treats walking and sustained hand contact as a coupled problem.

The preprint appeared on November 5. In simulation comparisons, cart-speed tracking error fell by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline. That is a maximum relative reduction in error, not an increase in robot speed. On a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, the simulation-trained controller pushed a cart carrying up to 30 kilograms at 0.5 metres per second without additional real-world training. Tests used a flat indoor floor. Relative cart heading came from an AprilTag, a visual marker recognised by a camera. The demonstration is not operation without external visual references or verified transport among unpredictable obstacles.

Thirty kilograms describes cargo on wheels, not a mass lifted by the hands. That distinction changes mechanical requirements and comparisons with other transport options. Floor and route properties, loading arrangements and human assistance still need evaluation. The source supplies no cost per trip, shift-level statistics or customer-site fleet-availability assessment.
